Health savings accounts pair tax-free saving with high-deductible health plans. The accounts began under a law effective in 2004. GAO-08-802T, testimony dated May 14, 2008, tracks who joins such plans, who opens an account, and how incomes compare with other filers.

Covered lives rose from about 438,000 in September 2004 to an estimated 6.1 million in January 2008. Filers citing account activity nearly tripled, to about 355,000 in 2005. Yet 42 to 49 percent of plan members never opened an account, often citing cost. Those who did open one earned far more on average, about $139,000 in 2005. That gap feeds debate over who the accounts truly help most.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-812t:
Extra help pays drug costs for poor Medicare members. The Social Security Administration runs sign-up for that low-income subsidy. GAO-08-812T, testimony dated May 22, 2008, counts who applied and who won aid, and asks why millions more have not applied.

Of about 7.2 million applicants, about 2.8 million won aid as of March 2008. In fiscal year 2007, about 570,000 won, 403,000 were denied, and 281,000 needed no decision. Too much income was the top denial reason. No solid data names all who qualify, so outreach flies partly blind. A tax data match is being tested to find them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-872t:
About 50 million Americans live with disabilities, served by a maze of federal programs. GAO-08-872T, testimony dated June 4, 2008, asks whether the data exist to judge how those people fare overall. It builds on GAO's May 2008 report on updating disability programs.

In 2005 GAO counted over 20 agencies and almost 200 programs for disabled people. Each counts its own wins, with its own goals and rules. No shared yardstick tracks health, work, or income across them all. National surveys also define disability in unlike ways, so the pieces will not join. Joint data work could fix that, GAO says.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-912t:
Health care costs drive the federal government's long-term money problem, GAO states in GAO-08-912T, June 2008 testimony. Updated simulations, using the 2008 trustees' projections, still show the long-term fiscal path as unsustainable despite deficit improvement from fiscal years 2003 to 2007. State and local governments face the same squeeze.

Social Security matters because of its size. But Medicare and Medicaid are both large and growing fast. That makes health spending the main driver over the long term. GAO makes four points. The outlook is a matter of utmost concern. Health costs drive it. Reform must be multipronged and reach beyond health care. And the window for phasing in fixes is shrinking even as pressures grow. Waiting, GAO warns, only makes the needed changes sharper.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-932t:
Pakistan's claims for war support payments get a hard look in GAO-08-932T, June 2008 testimony. The United States has repaid Pakistan about $5.56 billion in Coalition Support Funds for its counterterror work along the Afghan border. Pakistan takes 81 percent of all such payments. The testimony, drawn from a same-day report, asks whether the Defense Department applied its own claim-checking rules evenly.

It did not, GAO found. Guidance from 2003 requires claims to show costs above normal operations, proof the service happened, and papers backing the math. Broad reviews were done, but for many claims no one got the detailed proof. Over $2 billion paid for January 2004 through June 2007 claims could not be recalculated by a third party from the records kept. GAO urges tighter, steadier oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-962t:
Wage and hour law enforcement is thinning out, GAO-08-962T, July 2008 testimony, reports. The Fair Labor Standards Act protects over 130 million workers on minimum wage, overtime, and youth work limits. The Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division enforces it through investigations, partnerships, and outreach. Congress asked GAO to review trends from fiscal years 1997 to 2007 and how well the work is planned.

Enforcement actions fell by more than a third, from about 47,000 in 1997 to just under 30,000 in 2007. Longer full investigations, fewer investigators, and complaint screening explain much of the drop. About 72 percent of actions began with worker complaints. GAO found the division underusing its own data and outside input when planning, and reporting results unevenly. It recommends fuller use of both.
